cues.text: So, how does kagiboy actually work?
Let me take it apart for you.
Everything you see here is running live.
On the left, the real Game Boy ROM, written in C.
In the middle, the cartridge chip.
And on the right, the phone app.
Three parts.
And only one of them ever touches a key.
A Game Boy has no network.
No operating system.
Just the cartridge slot.
So that's our wire!
The ROM drops a command into a tiny mailbox in cartridge memory, and the chip writes its answer back.
The phone only ever talks to the chip, and only with public data.
Requests in, signatures out.
The phone is never trusted.
Your button mashing, and every shake, become entropy, mixed with the chip's own random generator.
Out come twelve standard words.
Solana keys on Phantom's path, EVM keys on MetaMask's, so they restore in any wallet you like.
Then you pick a PIN, and five wrong tries wipe the chip.
Pairing only happens while the Game Boy is listening.
The same six digits on both screens, press A, and you're paired.
Okay, now my favorite part.
The phone builds a normal Solana transfer and sends over the raw bytes.
The chip decodes them itself.
The fee payer has to be this wallet.
Exactly one instruction.
A plain System Program transfer.
Then the exact amount and the full address go on the screen.
You hold A for one second, the chip signs, and the phone just broadcasts.
And the phone can't fake a confirmation, either.
And here it is, live on devnet!
If the chip can't show something in full, it simply won't sign it.
No blind signing.
Token instructions, extra transfers, someone else paying the fee:
all refused.
The same key covers five EVM testnets, with a hard cap on fees.
Swaps come live from the SODAX SDK, but the cartridge checks every token against its own list and shows you the least you'll get.
In the demo, swaps are signed but never sent.
On the real cartridge, the keys move into an NXP secure element, and the ROM doesn't change at all.
It's all open source.
Go try it yourself at kagiboy.xyz/demo!
